structures.name: Eye
structures.summary: Detects light, movement, shape, and color in the surrounding water.
structures.detail: Fish eyes are adapted for underwater vision. Tilapia use sight to find food, avoid threats, and respond to other fish.

structures.name: Operculum
structures.summary: The firm gill cover protects the delicate gills and helps move water across them.
structures.detail: Movement of the operculum helps maintain a current of water over the gill filaments.

structures.name: Lateral line
structures.summary: Senses nearby water movement and low-frequency vibration.
structures.detail: A row of sensory organs along each side helps a fish orient, school, and detect movement even when visibility is poor.

structures.name: Dorsal fin
structures.summary: Helps stabilize the fish and resist rolling during swimming.
structures.detail: Tilapia have a long dorsal fin supported by spines and soft rays.

structures.name: Caudal fin
structures.summary: The tail fin provides the main forward thrust.
structures.detail: Side-to-side body waves transfer force to the caudal fin and push water backward, moving the fish forward.

structures.name: Pectoral fin
structures.summary: Supports steering, braking, hovering, and fine position changes.
structures.detail: The paired pectoral fins sit just behind the operculum and are especially useful during slow movement.

structures.name: Pelvic fin
structures.summary: Helps with balance, braking, and vertical positioning.
structures.detail: Tilapia have paired pelvic fins on the lower surface of the body.

structures.name: Anal fin
structures.summary: Adds stability and helps prevent unwanted rolling.
structures.detail: This unpaired fin is located behind the vent on the lower body.

structures.name: Vent
structures.summary: The external opening near the rear underside of the body.
structures.detail: The vent is a landmark used to show the direction of a supervised classroom incision in this simulation.

structures.name: Gills
structures.summary: Exchange dissolved oxygen and carbon dioxide between water and blood.
structures.detail: Many thin, well-supplied filaments create a large exchange surface. Water passes from the mouth across the gills and exits beneath the operculum.

structures.name: Heart
structures.summary: Pumps blood first toward the gills and then around the body.
structures.detail: The fish heart lies low and just behind the gills.

structures.name: Liver
structures.summary: Processes nutrients, stores energy, and produces bile used in digestion.
structures.detail: The liver is a prominent organ near the front of the body cavity and often partly covers other digestive organs.

structures.name: Stomach
structures.summary: Temporarily holds food and begins chemical and mechanical digestion.
structures.detail: Food reaches the stomach through the esophagus before moving into the intestine.

structures.name: Intestine
structures.summary: Continues digestion and absorbs nutrients before waste reaches the vent.
structures.detail: Tilapia are commonly omnivorous, and their intestine forms a long, folded pathway within the body cavity.

structures.name: Swim bladder
structures.summary: Helps the fish maintain depth without constant swimming.
structures.detail: This thin-walled gas-filled organ lies high in the body cavity, below the vertebral column and kidney.

structures.name: Kidney
structures.summary: Filters blood and helps control the balance of water and dissolved salts.
structures.detail: In bony fish, the kidney is a dark, narrow organ attached along the dorsal body wall.

structures.name: Gonad
structures.summary: Produces eggs in females or sperm in males.
structures.detail: Shape and size vary with sex and reproductive maturity. This neutral model represents the general location rather than a specific specimen.

structures.name: Vertebral column
structures.summary: Supports the body, protects the spinal cord, and anchors swimming muscles.
structures.detail: Repeated vertebrae form a flexible axis that bends during swimming.
